◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Finding the area enclosed by a spiral or a flower-petal curve is hard in x-y coordinates but elegant in polar form. The polar area formula sums up thin pie-slice sectors instead of rectangles — the right tool for curves that sweep around a center.

To find area in polar coordinates, you do not stack rectangles — you sum thin circular sectors (pie slices). Each tiny sector has area (1/2)r²dθ, which leads directly to the polar area integral.

The Polar Area Formula

Area in polar coordinates
The area swept by r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β is A = (1/2) ∫αβ r² dθ. Each thin sector contributes (1/2)r²dθ — the area of a slice of angle dθ.
🧠 ANALOGY

Cutting a pizza into ever-thinner slices: each slice is nearly a triangle with area (1/2)·radius²·angle. Add up all the slices as the angle sweeps around, and you have the total area. That is the polar area integral.

Figure 1. A thin polar sector of angle dθ and radius r. Its area is (1/2)r²dθ; integrating over the angle gives the enclosed area.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — area of a circle (polar)
Find the area enclosed by r = 3 (a circle) using the polar formula.
1
A = (1/2)∫02π r² dθ with r = 3, so r² = 9.
2
= (1/2)∫02π 9 dθ = (9/2)·[θ] from 0 to 2π.
3
= (9/2)(2π) = 9π.
A = 9π — exactly πr² = π(3²), confirming the formula matches the familiar circle area.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the area enclosed by the circle r = 5 using the polar area formula. Show your work.
Show worked solution

A = (1/2)∫02π 25 dθ = (25/2)(2π) = 25π. (Matches πr² = 25π.)

A = 25π
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the area of one half of the region for r = 2, i.e. A = (1/2)∫0π (2)² dθ (θ from 0 to π). Work below.
Show worked solution

r² = 4. A = (1/2)∫0π 4 dθ = (1/2)·4·[θ] from 0 to π = 2·π = 2π. (Half of the full circle area 4π — consistent.)

A = 2π
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Do not forget the 1/2 out front, and remember to square r. Also, choose the angle limits α to β carefully so you sweep the region exactly once — overshooting can double-count area on curves like cardioids and roses.

Key Takeaways
  • Polar area: A = (1/2)∫αβ r² dθ — sum of thin pie-slice sectors.
  • Each sector has area (1/2)r²dθ; don't drop the 1/2 or forget to square r.
  • The formula reproduces πr² for a full circle.
  • Pick the angle limits so the region is swept exactly once.

Polar details: the constant factor in front of the polar area integral is one-half, and polar arc length also involves the derivative dr/dtheta (not only for circles).

📊 FIGURE — Polar area comes in pie slices
A tiny wedge with angle dθ is almost a circular sector: area ½r²dθ. Sweep θ across the region and add slices: A = ∫½r(θ)²dθ. Note it is r SQUARED — the classic mistake is forgetting the square or the ½.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Polar coordinates locate points by distance and angle instead of by x and y. For anything with circular or rotational symmetry — spirals, flower-petal curves, planetary orbits, antenna patterns — polar coordinates make equations dramatically simpler.

In polar coordinates, a point is given by (r, θ): how far it is from the origin (r) and the angle θ from the positive x-axis. It is a different address system for the same plane.

Polar and Rectangular Conversion

Conversion formulas
From polar to rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. From rectangular to polar: r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.
🧠 ANALOGY

Rectangular coordinates are like giving directions as "3 blocks east, 4 blocks north." Polar coordinates say "head out at this angle for this distance" — like a radar bearing. Same destination, more natural when things rotate around a center.

Figure 1. A point in polar coordinates: r is the straight-line distance from the origin, θ is the angle from the positive x-axis.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — convert polar to rectangular
Convert the polar point (4, π/3) to rectangular coordinates.
1
x = r cos θ = 4 cos(π/3) = 4·(1/2) = 2.
2
y = r sin θ = 4 sin(π/3) = 4·(√3/2) = 2√3.
Rectangular: (2, 2√3) ≈ (2, 3.46).

Common Polar Curves

EquationCurve
r = aCircle of radius a centered at origin
r = a(1 + cos θ)Cardioid (heart shape)
r = a cos(nθ)Rose (petals)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Convert the polar point (2, π/2) to rectangular coordinates. Show your work.
Show worked solution

x = 2 cos(π/2) = 2·0 = 0. y = 2 sin(π/2) = 2·1 = 2.

(0, 2)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Convert the rectangular point (3, 4) to polar form: find r. (Use r = √(x² + y²).) Work below.
Show worked solution

r = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. (And θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927 rad.)

r = 5
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

When finding θ from tan θ = y/x, watch the quadrant — the arctangent alone cannot tell which of two opposite directions you mean. Check the signs of x and y to place θ in the correct quadrant.

Key Takeaways
  • Polar coordinates (r, θ) use distance and angle instead of x and y.
  • Convert with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ and r = √(x² + y²).
  • Polar form simplifies circular and rotational curves (circles, cardioids, roses).
  • Mind the quadrant when solving for θ.
📊 FIGURE — Polar coordinates: (r, θ) instead of (x, y)
A point is located by its distance r from the origin and the angle θ from the positive x-axis. Conversion: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and r² = x² + y². The dashed circles are curves of constant r — the polar "grid".

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Not every curve passes the vertical-line test — a circle, a spiral, the path of a projectile loop back on themselves. Parametric equations describe such curves by letting a parameter t (often time) drive both x and y. This is the natural language for motion and for curves that are not functions.

In parametric form, x and y are each functions of a third variable t: x = f(t), y = g(t). As t advances, the point (x, y) traces a curve — often a path through time.

Parametric Curves

Parametric equations
A curve given by x = f(t), y = g(t) for t in some interval. The parameter t determines both coordinates; eliminating t (when possible) recovers a relation between x and y.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of a GPS tracker on a moving car. At each moment t it records a position (x, y). The trail of dots is the parametric curve — and crucially, it carries direction and timing, not just shape. The same loop can be driven clockwise or counter-clockwise.

Example: x = cos t, y = sin t traces the unit circle as t goes from 0 to 2π (since cos²t + sin²t = 1).

Slope of a Parametric Curve

Parametric derivative
The slope is dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt) — divide the two rates. This works even where the curve is not a function of x.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — slope on a parametric curve
For x = t², y = t³, find dy/dx at t = 2.
1
Differentiate each with respect to t: dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 3t².
2
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t²/(2t) = (3/2)t.
3
At t = 2: (3/2)(2) = 3.
dy/dx = 3 at t = 2.

Parametric Arc Length

Arc length (parametric)
L = ∫ab √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — the parametric version of arc length, summing tiny hypotenuses as t runs from a to b.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. For x = t² , y = 2t, find dy/dx at t = 1. Show your work.
Show worked solution

dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2. dy/dx = 2/(2t) = 1/t. At t = 1: 1/1 = 1.

dy/dx = 1
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. For x = 3t, y = t², find dy/dx as a function of t. Work below.
Show worked solution

dx/dt = 3, dy/dt = 2t. dy/dx = 2t/3.

dy/dx = 2t/3
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The parametric slope is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) — a quotient of the two t-derivatives, not dy/dt times dx/dt and not their sum. A common slip is to forget the division.

Key Takeaways
  • Parametric equations x = f(t), y = g(t) trace curves that need not be functions of x.
  • Slope: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
  • Arc length: L = ∫√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.
  • The parameter encodes direction and timing, not just the curve's shape.

Components: dx/dt and dy/dt are the component velocities of the parametric motion — the rates of change of position, not the positions or accelerations themselves.

📊 FIGURE — A parametric curve is a journey, not just a shape
x and y are both driven by time t; the arrows show the direction of travel. Slopes come from the chain rule — dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) — and the curve can loop or cross itself, which ordinary y = f(x) graphs never do.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Once you know a few core series, you can manipulate them — substitute, differentiate, integrate — to get series for many more functions, without computing derivatives from scratch. This is how series for hard functions (and tricky integrals like ∫eˣ² dx) are found in practice.

The real power of Taylor series is that you can build new ones from old ones. Substitute, differentiate, or integrate a known series term by term — all valid within the radius of convergence.

Three Manipulations

OperationWhat it does
SubstituteReplace x with a new expression (e.g., x² or −x)
DifferentiateDifferentiate term by term to get the derivative's series
IntegrateIntegrate term by term — great for hard integrals
🧠 ANALOGY

Knowing the eˣ series is like owning a master template. Want eˣ²? Stamp x² into the template. Want the derivative? Adjust each piece. You reuse one known result many times instead of starting over.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — substitute into a known series
Find the Maclaurin series for ex².
1
Start with the known series eᵘ = 1 + u + u²/2! + u³/3! + ….
2
Substitute u = x²: ex² = 1 + x² + (x²)²/2! + (x²)³/3! + ….
3
Simplify the powers: 1 + x² + x⁴/2! + x⁶/3! + ….
ex² = Σ x2n/n! = 1 + x² + x⁴/2 + x⁶/6 + …. (This function has no elementary antiderivative, but its series integrates term by term easily!)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — approximate a value
Approximate e0.1 using the first three terms of the eˣ series.
1
eˣ ≈ 1 + x + x²/2. Set x = 0.1.
2
≈ 1 + 0.1 + (0.01)/2 = 1 + 0.1 + 0.005.
e0.1 ≈ 1.105. (True value ≈ 1.10517 — three terms already give four-figure accuracy.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the first three nonzero terms of the Maclaurin series for sin(x²), starting from sin u = u − u³/3! + u⁵/5! − …. Show your work.
Show worked solution

Substitute u = x²: sin(x²) = x² − (x²)³/3! + (x²)⁵/5! − … = x² − x⁶/6 + x¹⁰/120 − ….

x² − x⁶/6 + x¹⁰/120 − …
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Approximate cos(0.2) using the first two nonzero terms of the cos series (1 − x²/2). Work below.
Show worked solution

cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2. At x = 0.2: 1 − (0.04)/2 = 1 − 0.02 = 0.98. (True ≈ 0.980067.)

cos(0.2) ≈ 0.98
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

When you substitute, replace x everywhere and simplify the powers carefully: (x²)³ = x⁶, not x⁵. And these manipulations are only valid within the radius of convergence of the original series.

Key Takeaways
  • Build new series by substituting into known ones (e.g., u = x² in eᵘ).
  • You may differentiate and integrate a power series term by term.
  • Term-by-term integration handles integrals with no elementary antiderivative.
  • Truncating a series gives accurate numerical approximations.
📊 FIGURE — Taylor polynomials hugging sin x
The degree-1 Taylor polynomial (the tangent line, amber) matches sin x only near 0. Adding terms — x − x³/3! (green) — hugs the curve farther out. Each extra term buys agreement over a wider window; the full series equals sin x everywhere.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Taylor series express any smooth function as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives. This single idea powers numerical computation, physics approximations (small-angle, relativity), and much of applied math. It is one of the most far-reaching tools in all of calculus.

A Taylor series rebuilds a function from its value and all its derivatives at one point. Centered at 0, it gets the special name Maclaurin series.

The Taylor Series Formula

Taylor series
Near x = a, f(x) = Σn=0∞ [f(n)(a)/n!] (x − a)ⁿ = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + (f″(a)/2!)(x − a)² + …. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0.
🧠 ANALOGY

Building a Taylor series is like reconstructing a melody from its starting note plus its rate of change, its curvature, and so on. Each derivative adds one more layer of detail; with infinitely many layers you recover the exact tune (the function).

Key Maclaurin Series Worth Knowing

FunctionMaclaurin series
eˣ1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …
sin xx − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
cos x1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …
1/(1 − x)1 + x + x² + x³ + … (|x| < 1)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — build the series for eˣ
Find the Maclaurin series of f(x) = eˣ.
1
Every derivative of eˣ is eˣ, so f(n)(0) = e⁰ = 1 for all n.
2
Plug into the formula: Σ [1/n!] xⁿ.
3
Write it out: 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ….
eˣ = Σn=0∞ xⁿ/n!, valid for all x. (Setting x = 1 even gives a series for e itself.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Write the first four nonzero terms of the Maclaurin series for cos x. Then state the general pattern. Show your work.
Show worked solution

cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − x⁶/6! + …. Only even powers appear, with alternating signs: Σ(−1)ⁿ x2n/(2n)!.

1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − x⁶/6! + …
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Use the geometric-series formula 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + … to write the first four terms of the series for 1/(1 − 2x). (Replace x with 2x.) Work below.
Show worked solution

Substitute 2x for x: 1 + (2x) + (2x)² + (2x)³ + … = 1 + 2x + 4x² + 8x³ + ….

1 + 2x + 4x² + 8x³ + …
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Do not drop the factorials in the denominators — they are what make the series converge. And remember the patterns: sin x uses only odd powers, cos x only even powers, both with alternating signs.

Key Takeaways
  • Taylor series: f(x) = Σ [f(n)(a)/n!](x − a)ⁿ; Maclaurin is centered at a = 0.
  • Memorize the series for eˣ, sin x, cos x, and 1/(1 − x).
  • sin uses odd powers, cos uses even powers, both alternating.
  • The factorials in the denominators are essential.
📊 FIGURE — Taylor polynomials hugging sin x
The degree-1 Taylor polynomial (the tangent line, amber) matches sin x only near 0. Adding terms — x − x³/3! (green) — hugs the curve farther out. Each extra term buys agreement over a wider window; the full series equals sin x everywhere.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A power series is an "infinite polynomial" — and it lets us represent complicated functions (eˣ, sin x) as sums of simple powers. This is how calculators actually compute these functions, and the gateway to Taylor series. First we must know where such a series converges.

A power series is a series whose terms contain powers of x: Σcₙxⁿ. For some x-values it converges; for others it diverges. The set where it converges is an interval, and its half-width is the radius of convergence.

Power Series and Convergence

Power series
A series of the form Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ centered at a. It converges for x within a distance R of the center — the radius of convergence — giving an interval of convergence from a − R to a + R.
🧠 ANALOGY

A power series is like a radio signal centered at a: it comes through clearly only within a certain range R of the tower. Inside that radius the series converges; outside, it breaks up (diverges). The edges of the range need to be checked individually.

Finding the Radius with the Ratio Test

Apply the ratio test to |cₙ₊₁xⁿ⁺¹ / cₙxⁿ| and require the limit < 1. Solving for |x| gives the radius R.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — radius and interval
Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n.
1
Ratio test: |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = |xn+1/(n+1)| · |n/xⁿ| = |x|·n/(n+1).
2
Limit as n → ∞: |x|·1 = |x|. Require |x| < 1 for convergence, so R = 1.
3
Check endpoints. At x = 1: Σ1/n (harmonic) diverges. At x = −1: Σ(−1)ⁿ/n (alternating harmonic) converges.
Radius R = 1; interval of convergence [−1, 1) — including −1 but excluding 1.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n!. (Apply the ratio test; recall it gave 0 earlier for a related series.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

|aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = |xn+1/(n+1)!|·|n!/xⁿ| = |x|/(n+1) → 0 for every x. Since the limit is 0 < 1 for all x, it converges everywhere: R = ∞.

R = ∞ (converges for all x)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find the radius of convergence of Σ 2ⁿxⁿ. (Ratio test.) Work below.
Show worked solution

|aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = |2n+1xn+1|/|2ⁿxⁿ| = 2|x|. Require 2|x| < 1 → |x| < 1/2. So R = 1/2.

R = 1/2
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The ratio test gives the radius but is inconclusive at the endpoints (where |x| = R). You must test x = a − R and x = a + R separately with another test to get the full interval of convergence.

Key Takeaways
  • A power series Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ converges within a radius R of its center a.
  • Find R with the ratio test: require the limit of |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| < 1.
  • The interval of convergence spans a − R to a + R.
  • Always test the endpoints separately.
📊 FIGURE — The interval of convergence
A power series converges absolutely inside a symmetric radius R around its center a, diverges outside, and each ENDPOINT must be tested by hand — one may converge while the other diverges. The ratio test finds R; endpoint checks finish the job.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The ratio test is the workhorse for series with factorials or exponentials — and it is exactly the tool that finds the radius of convergence of a power series in the next chapter. It often succeeds where comparison is hard.

The ratio test examines how each term compares to the one before. If terms shrink fast enough (ratio less than 1), the series converges. It is especially powerful for factorials and powers.

The Ratio Test

Ratio test
Compute L = limn→∞ |aₙ₊₁ / aₙ|. Then: L < 1 → converges (absolutely); L > 1 → diverges; L = 1 → inconclusive (try another test).
🧠 ANALOGY

The ratio L is the "shrink factor" between consecutive terms. If each term is reliably less than the previous (L < 1) — like a geometric series with ratio less than 1 — the sum stays finite. If terms grow (L > 1), the sum explodes.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a factorial series
Does Σ 2ⁿ/n! converge?
1
aₙ = 2ⁿ/n!, so aₙ₊₁ = 2n+1/(n+1)!.
2
Ratio: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = [2n+1/(n+1)!]·[n!/2ⁿ] = 2/(n+1).
3
L = limn→∞ 2/(n+1) = 0, which is < 1.
Since L = 0 < 1, the series converges. (Factorials grow so fast they crush the exponential.)

The Root Test

Root test
Compute L = limn→∞ n√|aₙ|. Same conclusion as the ratio test: L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive. Best when aₙ is an nth power.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Apply the ratio test to Σ 1/n!. (Find aₙ₊₁/aₙ and its limit.) Converge or diverge? Show your work.
Show worked solution

aₙ = 1/n!, aₙ₊₁ = 1/(n+1)!. Ratio = n!/(n+1)! = 1/(n+1). L = lim 1/(n+1) = 0 < 1. Converges.

Converges (L = 0)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Apply the ratio test to Σ 3ⁿ/n. (Compute the limit of |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|.) Work below.
Show worked solution

aₙ = 3ⁿ/n. Ratio = [3n+1/(n+1)]·[n/3ⁿ] = 3n/(n+1). L = lim 3n/(n+1) = 3 > 1. Diverges.

Diverges (L = 3 > 1)
✐ PRACTICE — when it fails
Problem 3. Apply the ratio test to Σ 1/n². What is L, and what does the test tell you? Work below.
Show worked solution

Ratio = n²/(n+1)². L = lim n²/(n+1)² = 1. The ratio test is inconclusive — but we already know Σ1/n² converges by the p-series rule (p = 2).

L = 1, inconclusive (use the p-series rule: converges)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

When L = 1, the ratio test tells you nothing — you must switch tests. This is exactly the case for p-series (the ratio always limits to 1), so reach for the p-rule or comparison instead.

Key Takeaways
  • Ratio test: L = lim|aₙ₊₁/aₙ|; L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive.
  • Best for series with factorials or exponentials.
  • Root test: L = lim n√|aₙ|, same rules — best for nth powers.
  • When L = 1, use a different test (often the p-series rule).
📊 FIGURE — The ratio test reads like a speedometer
Compute L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| — the series’ long-run shrink factor. Below 1 it behaves like a convergent geometric series; above 1 the terms eventually GROW, so it diverges; exactly 1 tells you nothing (try another test). Factorials and exponentials love this test.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Series whose signs alternate (+, −, +, −) converge more readily than all-positive ones, because successive terms partly cancel. Understanding them — and the distinction between absolute and conditional convergence — is essential for power series and for knowing when you can safely rearrange terms.

An alternating series flips sign each term. Cancellation makes convergence easier, and a beautifully simple test handles them.

The Alternating Series Test

Alternating series test
An alternating series Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ (with bₙ > 0) converges if two conditions hold: (1) the terms decrease, bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ, and (2) bₙ → 0. Both are required.
🧠 ANALOGY

Imagine stepping forward 1, back 1/2, forward 1/3, back 1/4… Each step is smaller and reverses direction, so you zero in on a single spot rather than wandering off. Shrinking, alternating steps converge to a point.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — the alternating harmonic series
Does 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converge?
1
This is Σ(−1)n+1(1/n), alternating with bₙ = 1/n.
2
Check (1): 1/(n+1) < 1/n — terms decrease. ✓
3
Check (2): lim 1/n = 0. ✓
Both conditions hold, so it converges. (Remarkably, the non-alternating Σ1/n diverges — the alternating signs rescue it. Its sum is ln 2.)

Absolute vs Conditional Convergence

Absolute vs conditional
A series converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges. If Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it converges conditionally. Absolute convergence is the stronger, more robust property.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — classify the convergence
Is the alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … absolutely or conditionally convergent?
1
It converges (shown above).
2
Take absolute values: Σ|(−1)n+1/n| = Σ1/n — the harmonic series, which diverges.
It converges but not absolutely, so it is conditionally convergent.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Does Σ (−1)ⁿ/n² converge? Apply the alternating series test (check both conditions). Show your work.
Show worked solution

bₙ = 1/n². Decreasing: 1/(n+1)² < 1/n². ✓ Limit: 1/n² → 0. ✓ Both hold, so it converges. (It is also absolutely convergent, since Σ1/n² converges.)

Converges (in fact absolutely)
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. The series Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n converges by the alternating series test. Is it absolutely or conditionally convergent? (Check Σ1/√n.) Work below.
Show worked solution

Σ|(−1)ⁿ/√n| = Σ1/√n = Σ1/n1/2, a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, which diverges. So the original converges but not absolutely → conditional.

Conditionally convergent
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The alternating series test needs both conditions — decreasing terms and terms going to 0. If the terms do not approach 0, the divergence test already kills the series. Do not skip checking the decreasing condition.

Key Takeaways
  • Alternating series test: converges if terms decrease and → 0.
  • Absolute convergence: Σ|aₙ| converges (the strong, robust kind).
  • Conditional convergence: Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges (e.g., alternating harmonic).
  • Both conditions of the alternating series test are required.
📊 FIGURE — Partial sums of an alternating series
Each term overshoots the limit in the opposite direction, but the overshoots shrink — the partial sums zigzag inward and squeeze onto the sum L. This is why the alternating series test only needs terms decreasing to 0, and why the error is at most the first omitted term.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

If a series looks like one you already understand, you can settle its fate by comparison. These tests let you leverage the p-series and geometric series you know to decide messy-looking series — a fast, intuitive tool.

If your series resembles a known one, compare them. A series with smaller positive terms than a convergent series must also converge; one with larger terms than a divergent series must also diverge.

The Direct Comparison Test

Direct comparison test
For positive-term series: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges (smaller than convergent). If aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 and Σbₙ diverges, then Σaₙ diverges (bigger than divergent).
🧠 ANALOGY

If your spending is always less than a friend whose budget is finite, your spending is finite too. If it is always more than someone who spends without limit, yours is unlimited as well. Comparison bounds your series between behaviors you already understand.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — direct comparison
Does Σ 1/(n² + 1) converge?
1
Compare to bₙ = 1/n². Since n² + 1 > n², we have 1/(n² + 1) < 1/n².
2
Σ 1/n² is a convergent p-series (p = 2 > 1).
3
Our terms are smaller than a convergent series' terms.
By direct comparison, Σ 1/(n² + 1) converges.

The Limit Comparison Test

Limit comparison test
If aₙ, bₙ > 0 and limn→∞ (aₙ/bₙ) = L where 0 < L < ∞, then Σaₙ and Σbₙ both converge or both diverge. Useful when the inequality for direct comparison is awkward.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — limit comparison
Does Σ 1/(2n + 3) converge?
1
For large n, this behaves like 1/(2n), i.e. like 1/n. Compare to bₙ = 1/n.
2
lim (aₙ/bₙ) = lim [1/(2n+3)]/[1/n] = lim n/(2n+3) = 1/2, which is between 0 and ∞.
3
Σ 1/n (harmonic) diverges, so our series shares that fate.
By limit comparison, Σ 1/(2n + 3) diverges.

Converges
✐ PRACTICE — you try it

lim [1/(3n−1)]/[1/n] = lim n/(3n−1) = 1/3 (between 0 and ∞). Σ1/n diverges, so this diverges too.

Diverges
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Most series are not geometric, so you need convergence tests. The integral test cleverly links a series to an improper integral you already know how to evaluate, and it gives the hugely useful p-series rule as a free bonus.

The integral test compares a series Σf(n) to the integral ∫f(x) dx. Since a series is a sum of rectangle areas and the integral is the area under the curve, the two converge or diverge together.

The Integral Test

Integral test
If f is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ 1, then Σn=1∞ f(n) and ∫1∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge. Evaluate the (easier) integral to decide the series.
🧠 ANALOGY

Picture the series terms as rectangle areas standing on the curve y = f(x). The total rectangle area (the series) and the smooth area under the curve (the integral) trap each other — if one is finite, so is the other. They share the same fate.

The p-Series Rule

p-series
A series of the form Σ 1/np. It converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1 — derived directly from the integral test and the p-test for integrals.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — the harmonic series
Does the harmonic series Σ 1/n converge?
1
This is a p-series with p = 1. Apply the integral test with f(x) = 1/x.
2
∫1∞ (1/x) dx = limt→∞ ln t = ∞ — the integral diverges.
3
So the series diverges too. (Consistent with the p-rule: p = 1 ≤ 1.)
The harmonic series diverges — famously, even though its terms shrink to 0.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a convergent p-series
Does Σ 1/n² converge?
1
p-series with p = 2.
2
Since p = 2 > 1, the p-rule says it converges.
Σ 1/n² converges. (Its sum is the famous π²/6, though the rule only tells us it is finite.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Does Σ 1/n³ converge or diverge? State the value of p and your reasoning. Show your work.
Show worked solution

p-series with p = 3. Since 3 > 1, it converges by the p-rule.

Converges (p = 3 > 1)

Diverges (p = 1/2 ≤ 1)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

An infinite series adds up infinitely many terms — and astonishingly, the total can be finite. Geometric series are the most important example, appearing in finance (annuities), physics (bouncing balls), and as the building block for power series later.

A series is the sum of a sequence's terms: a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + …. To make sense of an infinite sum, look at the partial sums and ask whether they converge.

Series and Partial Sums

Convergence of a series
The partial sum Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. The series converges to S if the partial sums Sₙ → S as n → ∞. Otherwise it diverges.

Geometric Series

Geometric series
A series where each term is a constant ratio r times the previous: a + ar + ar² + ar³ + …. It converges if |r| < 1, to the sum S = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, it diverges.
🧠 ANALOGY

Walk half the remaining distance to a wall, then half of what is left, then half again… You take infinitely many steps but travel a finite total distance — you reach the wall. That is a geometric series with r = 1/2 summing to a finite value, even with infinitely many terms.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — sum a geometric series
Find the sum of 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ….
1
First term a = 1; ratio r = 1/2 (each term is half the previous).
2
Since |r| = 1/2 < 1, it converges. Use S = a/(1 − r).
3
S = 1/(1 − 1/2) = 1/(1/2) = 2.
The infinite sum is 2 — a finite total from infinitely many terms.

The Divergence Test

Divergence test (nth-term test)
If limn→∞ aₙ ≠ 0, the series Σaₙ diverges. (Caution: if the limit is 0, the test is inconclusive — the series might still diverge.)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — divergence test
Does Σ n/(n + 1) converge?
1
Check the term limit: limn→∞ n/(n + 1) = 1, not 0.
2
Since the terms do not shrink to 0, the divergence test applies.
The series diverges — you cannot get a finite sum when the terms keep adding nearly 1 each.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the sum of the geometric series 3 + 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + …. (Identify a and r, then use a/(1 − r).) Show your work.
Show worked solution

a = 3, r = 1/3 (each term is one-third the previous). |r| < 1, so S = 3/(1 − 1/3) = 3/(2/3) = 9/2.

S = 9/2 = 4.5
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Use the divergence test on Σ (2n)/(n + 5). Does it converge or diverge? Work below.
Show worked solution

limn→∞ 2n/(n + 5) = 2 ≠ 0. By the divergence test, the series diverges.

Diverges (term limit = 2 ≠ 0)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The divergence test is one-directional: term limit ≠ 0 proves divergence, but term limit = 0 proves nothing. The harmonic series Σ1/n has terms going to 0 yet diverges. Never conclude convergence from the divergence test alone.

Key Takeaways
  • A series converges if its partial sums approach a finite limit.
  • Geometric series: converges if |r| < 1, with sum a/(1 − r).
  • Divergence test: if aₙ ↛ 0, the series diverges.
  • Term limit = 0 is inconclusive — more tests are needed.

Fill a unit square: take half, then half of what remains, then half again. The pieces never overlap and never escape the square — the geometric series with r = ½ converges to exactly 1. In general Σarⁿ = a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1.

A sequence is an infinite ordered list of numbers, and the central question is where its terms are headed. This is the foundation for infinite series (the rest of this chapter) and for understanding limits of discrete processes — interest compounding, iterative algorithms, population steps.

A sequence is just a list of numbers in order: a₁, a₂, a₃, …, with a rule for the nth term aₙ. The key question is whether the terms converge to some limit as n grows.

Convergence of a Sequence

Sequence limit
A sequence {aₙ} converges to L if aₙ approaches L as n → ∞, written limn→∞ aₙ = L. If no finite limit exists, the sequence diverges.
🧠 ANALOGY

A sequence is like a series of measurements taken at steps 1, 2, 3, … If the readings settle toward a steady value (a thermometer approaching room temperature), the sequence converges. If they keep growing or bouncing, it diverges.

You evaluate sequence limits with the same tools as function limits — including the highest-power comparison for rational expressions:

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a convergent sequence
Does aₙ = n/(n + 1) converge? If so, to what?
1
Look at the behavior as n → ∞. Divide top and bottom by n: 1/(1 + 1/n).
2
As n → ∞, the 1/n → 0, leaving 1/(1 + 0).
3
= 1.
The sequence converges to 1. (Terms: 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, … creeping up toward 1.)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a divergent sequence
Does aₙ = 2ⁿ converge?
1
Terms: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … — they grow without bound.
2
limn→∞ 2ⁿ = ∞, not a finite number.
The sequence diverges (to infinity).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find limn→∞ (3n + 1)/(n + 2), or state that the sequence diverges. Show your work.
Show worked solution

Divide by n: (3 + 1/n)/(1 + 2/n). As n → ∞, the 1/n terms vanish: 3/1 = 3.

Converges to 3
✐ PRACTICE — you try it

Show worked solution

As n → ∞, n² → ∞, so 1/n² → 0. Terms 1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16, … shrink to 0.

Converges to 0
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Do not confuse a sequence (the list of terms) with a series (their sum). The sequence 1/n converges to 0, but the series Σ1/n diverges. Asking "where do the terms go?" is different from "what do they add up to?"

Key Takeaways
  • A sequence is an ordered list aₙ; it converges if limn→∞ aₙ is a finite number.
  • Evaluate sequence limits like function limits (highest-power comparison, etc.).
  • Growing-without-bound or oscillating sequences diverge.
  • A sequence is not a series — terms approaching 0 does not mean the sum is finite.

A sequence is a function whose domain is the positive integers — that is the whole definition, and it is what makes aₙ discrete rather than a curve. Keep it distinct from a series, which is the sum of those terms: a sequence converges when its terms settle, a series when its partial sums do.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When a force varies as an object moves — stretching a spring, lifting a hanging chain, pumping water from a tank — you cannot use simple "force times distance." Integration adds up the work over each tiny displacement. This is calculus directly powering physics and engineering.

Work is force times distance — but only when the force is constant. When the force changes with position, you integrate: add up F·dx over every tiny step.

Work with a Variable Force

Work integral
If a force F(x) acts along the x-direction from a to b, the work done is W = ∫ab F(x) dx. Each tiny displacement dx requires work F(x)·dx; the integral sums them.
🧠 ANALOGY

Stretching a spring gets harder the farther you pull — the force is not constant. So you cannot just multiply. Instead, total the small bits of effort over each millimeter of stretch. That running total is the work integral.

Hooke's Law for Springs

Hooke's Law
A spring resists with force F(x) = kx, proportional to the stretch x (k is the spring constant). The work to stretch from 0 to d is W = ∫0d kx dx = (1/2)kd².

Force at stretch x: F(x) = 200x.

3
= 100·(0.5)² = 100·0.25 = 25.
W = 25 joules. (The (1/2)kd² shortcut gives the same: 0.5·200·0.25 = 25 J.)

W = 8 joules

Only use W = force × distance when the force is constant. For a spring or any position-dependent force, you must integrate. Using F·d with a varying force (e.g., taking the maximum force) overcounts the work badly.

How long is a curve? How much material covers a curved surface? Arc length and surface area of revolution answer these — essential for everything from measuring cable to manufacturing curved panels and computing fuel-tank surface area.

A curve's length comes from adding up tiny straight segments. Each segment's length, by the Pythagorean theorem, involves the slope — which is why the derivative appears under a square root.

Arc Length

Arc length
The length of y = f(x) from a to b is L = ∫ab √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx. Each tiny piece of curve is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs dx and dy = f′(x)dx.
🧠 ANALOGY

Walk a winding trail in tiny steps. Each step covers some horizontal distance dx and some vertical rise dy; the actual step length is √(dx² + dy²). Add up every step and you get the trail's true length — longer than the straight-line distance, because of all the up-and-down.

Figure 1. A small piece of the curve is nearly a straight line — the hypotenuse √(dx² + dy²) of a tiny triangle. Summing them gives the arc-length integral.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — arc length
Find the length of y = (2/3)x3/2 from x = 0 to x = 3.
1
f′(x) = (2/3)·(3/2)x1/2 = x1/2. So [f′]² = x.
2
L = ∫03 √(1 + x) dx.
3
Antiderivative of (1 + x)1/2 is (2/3)(1 + x)3/2. Evaluate from 0 to 3: (2/3)(43/2 − 13/2) = (2/3)(8 − 1) = 14/3.
L = 14/3 ≈ 4.67 units.

Surface Area of Revolution

Surface area
Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis generates a surface of area S = ∫ab 2π f(x) √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx — the arc-length element times the circumference 2πf(x) it sweeps.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Set up the arc-length integral for y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1. (You do not need to evaluate it — just write the integral correctly.) Work below.
Show worked solution

f′(x) = 2x, so [f′]² = 4x². L = ∫01 √(1 + 4x²) dx. (This particular integral needs trig substitution to evaluate, but the setup is the key skill.)

L = ∫01 √(1 + 4x²) dx
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the arc length of y = (2/3)x3/2 from x = 0 to x = 8. (Same form as the worked example; [f′]² = x.) Work below.
Show worked solution

L = ∫08√(1 + x)dx = (2/3)(1 + x)3/2 from 0 to 8 = (2/3)(93/2 − 1) = (2/3)(27 − 1) = 52/3 ≈ 17.3.

L = 52/3 ≈ 17.3
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The "1 +" under the root is not optional — it comes from the horizontal leg dx of each tiny triangle. Writing √([f′]²) = f′ (dropping the 1) is wrong and would give the wrong length entirely.

Some solids of revolution are far easier to handle with cylindrical shells than with washers — especially when revolving around the y-axis. Knowing both methods means you can always pick the one that makes the integral simple.

The shell method slices a solid into thin concentric cylindrical shells, like the layers of an onion. Each shell, unrolled, is a thin rectangular sheet whose area is circumference × height.

The Shell Method

Shell method
Revolving around the y-axis, each shell at position x has radius x and height f(x). Its volume is 2π·(radius)·(height)·(thickness). Total: V = ∫ab 2π x · f(x) dx.

1
Each shell has radius x and height f(x) = x².
2
V = ∫02 2π x · x² dx = 2π∫02 x³ dx.
3
= 2π[x⁴/4] from 0 to 2 = 2π(16/4) = 2π·4 = 8π.
V = 8π cubic units.

Show worked solution

V = 18π

Spin a flat region around an axis and you get a 3-D solid — a sphere, a cone, a vase. The disk and washer methods compute the volume of any such solid of revolution. This is how engineers find the volume of turned parts, tanks, and lenses.

When you revolve a region around an axis, you can slice the resulting solid into thin disks (or washers, if there is a hole). Each slice is a circle; integrate their areas to get the volume.

The Disk Method

Disk method
Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis, each slice is a disk of radius R(x) = f(x) and area πR². The volume is V = ∫ab π[f(x)]² dx.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of the solid as a stack of coins of varying radius. Each coin is a disk with area π·radius² and a tiny thickness dx. Stack (integrate) them up and you have the total volume — exactly what a lathe builds up as it turns a shape.

1
Radius of each disk: R(x) = √x. So R² = x.

= π[x²/2] from 0 to 4 = π(16/2 − 0) = 8π.

  • Each slice's area is π·radius²; integrate along the axis of revolution.
  • Square the radius; subtract squared radii (not the squared difference).

Spin the region under the curve around the x-axis: each vertical sliver sweeps a DISK of radius f(x) and thickness dx, so its volume is π f(x)² dx. Add the slices: V = ∫ π f(x)² dx. A washer subtracts an inner hole: π(R² − r²) dx.

Some integrals run to infinity — ∫1∞ — or have an integrand that blows up. Remarkably, an infinitely long region can still have finite area. Improper integrals make this precise, and they underpin probability (total probability = 1) and many physics results.

An improper integral has an infinite limit of integration or an integrand that becomes infinite. You handle it by replacing the trouble with a variable and taking a limit.

The Definition

Improper integral (infinite limit)
∫a∞ f(x) dx = limt→∞ ∫at f(x) dx. If the limit is a finite number, the integral converges; if it is infinite or does not exist, it diverges.
🧠 ANALOGY

Picture an infinitely long horn that gets thin so fast it holds only a finite amount of paint. Counterintuitive, but real: if a function shrinks quickly enough, the area beneath its infinite tail can still total a finite number. Convergence is exactly that "shrinks fast enough" condition.

Figure 1. The region stretches to infinity, yet if the curve drops quickly enough the shaded area converges to a finite value.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a convergent integral
Evaluate ∫1∞ 1/x² dx.
1
Rewrite with a limit: limt→∞ ∫1t x−2 dx.
2
Antiderivative of x−2 is −x−1 = −1/x. Evaluate from 1 to t: (−1/t) − (−1/1) = 1 − 1/t.
3
Take the limit: limt→∞ (1 − 1/t) = 1 − 0 = 1.
∫1∞ 1/x² dx = 1 — it converges.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a divergent integral
Evaluate ∫1∞ 1/x dx.
1
limt→∞ ∫1t (1/x) dx. Antiderivative is ln|x|.
2
Evaluate: ln t − ln 1 = ln t.
3
limt→∞ ln t = ∞.
∫1∞ 1/x dx diverges. (Notice how close 1/x and 1/x² look, yet one converges and the other does not — the rate of decay is decisive.)
💡 TIP — the p-test

For ∫1∞ 1/xp dx: it converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1. That instantly explains why 1/x² (p = 2) converges but 1/x (p = 1) diverges.

✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Evaluate ∫1∞ 1/x³ dx using a limit. Does it converge? Show your work.
Show worked solution

limt→∞ ∫1t x−3 dx. Antiderivative −x−2/2 = −1/(2x²). Evaluate: −1/(2t²) − (−1/2) = 1/2 − 1/(2t²). Limit → 1/2. Converges (p = 3 > 1).

∫ = 1/2 (converges)
✐ PRACTICE — use the p-test
Problem 2. Without fully computing, state whether ∫1∞ 1/√x dx converges or diverges, and why. Work below.
Show worked solution

1/√x = 1/x1/2, so p = 1/2. Since p ≤ 1, the p-test says it diverges.

Diverges (p = 1/2 ≤ 1)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

You cannot just "plug in ∞" — you must write the integral as a limit and evaluate it properly. Treating ∞ like a number is the most common error, and it hides the difference between convergence and divergence.

Key Takeaways
  • Improper integrals have infinite limits or unbounded integrands; evaluate with a limit.
  • Converges = finite value; diverges = infinite or nonexistent.
  • p-test: ∫1∞ 1/xp converges if p > 1, diverges if p ≤ 1.
  • Never substitute ∞ directly — always take the limit.
📊 FIGURE — An improper integral: infinite region, finite area
The region under 1/x² from 1 to ∞ never ends — yet its area is exactly 1, because ∫₁ᵇ x⁻²dx = 1 − 1/b → 1. Improper integrals are limits of ordinary ones. Compare 1/x: its tail integral grows like ln b and DIVERGES. The boundary case is the p-test.

A complicated rational function like 1/((x−1)(x+2)) has no obvious antiderivative — but if you split it into simple pieces, each integrates to a logarithm in one step. Partial fractions is that splitting technique, and it is essential for integrating rational functions (and later, for Laplace transforms).

Adding fractions combines them over a common denominator. Partial fraction decomposition runs that process backward: it breaks one complicated fraction into a sum of simple ones, each easy to integrate.

The Idea

Partial fraction decomposition
Write a proper rational function as a sum of fractions with simpler denominators. For distinct linear factors, each factor (x − r) gets its own term A/(x − r) with a constant to be found.
🧠 ANALOGY

If a recipe calls for "1.5 cups," it is easier to measure as "1 cup + ½ cup." Partial fractions does the same to a messy fraction — rewrites it as a sum of bite-sized pieces, each of which you already know how to handle.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — distinct linear factors
Find ∫ 1/((x − 1)(x + 2)) dx.
1
Set up the decomposition: 1/((x−1)(x+2)) = A/(x−1) + B/(x+2).
2
Multiply through by (x−1)(x+2): 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1).
3
Plug in clever values. x = 1: 1 = A(3) → A = 1/3. x = −2: 1 = B(−3) → B = −1/3.
4
Integrate each piece: (1/3)∫dx/(x−1) − (1/3)∫dx/(x+2) = (1/3)ln|x−1| − (1/3)ln|x+2|.
∫ = (1/3)ln|x − 1| − (1/3)ln|x + 2| + C, which can be written (1/3)ln|(x−1)/(x+2)| + C.

The Setup Rules

Denominator factorContributes
Distinct linear (x − r)A/(x − r)
Repeated linear (x − r)²A/(x − r) + B/(x − r)²
Irreducible quadratic (x² + bx + c)(Ax + B)/(x² + bx + c)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Decompose and integrate ∫ 1/((x)(x + 1)) dx. (Set up A/x + B/(x+1).) Show your work.
Show worked solution

1/(x(x+1)) = A/x + B/(x+1). Multiply: 1 = A(x+1) + Bx. x = 0: A = 1. x = −1: 1 = B(−1) → B = −1. Integrate: ∫(1/x − 1/(x+1))dx = ln|x| − ln|x+1| + C.

∫ = ln|x| − ln|x + 1| + C
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find A and B for 5/((x − 2)(x + 3)) = A/(x − 2) + B/(x + 3). Work below.
Show worked solution

5 = A(x + 3) + B(x − 2). x = 2: 5 = A(5) → A = 1. x = −3: 5 = B(−5) → B = −1.

A = 1, B = −1
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Partial fractions requires a proper fraction (numerator degree < denominator degree). If the top degree is equal or higher, do polynomial long division first, then decompose the remainder. Skipping that step gives wrong results.

Key Takeaways
  • Partial fractions splits a rational function into simpler, integrable pieces.
  • Each distinct linear factor (x − r) contributes A/(x − r); each piece integrates to a log.
  • Find the constants by clearing denominators and plugging in strategic x-values.
  • If the fraction is improper, do long division first.
📊 FIGURE — Partial fractions: un-add the fraction
A rational function with a factorable denominator is the SUM of simpler pieces — one unknown constant per linear factor (repeated factors get a term per power; irreducible quadratics get Bx + C). Solve for A and B, then integrate each piece as a log.

Integrals containing √(a² − x²), √(a² + x²), or √(x² − a²) resist every earlier method. Trig substitution replaces x with a trig function so the Pythagorean identity collapses the square root — turning an impossible-looking integral into a trig integral you can solve.

When a square root of a quadratic blocks your integral, substitute a trig function for x. The right choice makes the expression under the root into a perfect square (via sin²+cos²=1), and the root disappears.

The Three Forms

ExpressionSubstituteIdentity used
√(a² − x²)x = a sin θ1 − sin²θ = cos²θ
√(a² + x²)x = a tan θ1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
√(x² − a²)x = a sec θsec²θ − 1 = tan²θ
🧠 ANALOGY

Each form matches a right triangle. √(a² − x²) is a leg when x and a are the other leg and hypotenuse — so setting x = a sin θ just names the angle. You are reading the integral off a triangle instead of fighting the algebra.

Figure 1. For √(a² − x²): set x = a sin θ. Then the hypotenuse is a, the opposite leg is x, and the adjacent leg is √(a² − x²) = a cos θ — the root simplifies instantly.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — the a² − x² form
Find ∫ dx/√(4 − x²).
1
Here a² = 4, so a = 2. Substitute x = 2 sin θ, dx = 2 cos θ dθ.
2
Then 4 − x² = 4 − 4sin²θ = 4cos²θ, so √(4 − x²) = 2 cos θ.
3
The integral becomes ∫ (2 cos θ dθ)/(2 cos θ) = ∫ 1 dθ = θ + C.
4
Since x = 2 sin θ, θ = arcsin(x/2).
∫ dx/√(4 − x²) = arcsin(x/2) + C.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find ∫ dx/√(9 − x²) using x = 3 sin θ. Show your work, then convert back.
Show worked solution

a = 3, x = 3 sin θ, dx = 3 cos θ dθ. 9 − x² = 9cos²θ → √ = 3 cos θ. Integral = ∫(3 cos θ)/(3 cos θ) dθ = ∫dθ = θ + C = arcsin(x/3) + C.

∫ = arcsin(x/3) + C
✐ PRACTICE — identify the form
Problem 2. Which trig substitution would you use for ∫ dx/√(x² + 16), and what is x equal to? Explain in the space below.
Show worked solution

This is the √(a² + x²) form with a² = 16, a = 4. Use x = 4 tan θ, because 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ makes 16 + x² = 16sec²θ, so the root becomes 4 sec θ.

Use x = 4 tan θ (the √(a²+x²) case)

Do not forget to convert your answer back to x using a right triangle. An answer left in θ is incomplete. Draw the triangle from your substitution to read off sin θ, cos θ, or tan θ in terms of x.

Key Takeaways

  • The matching Pythagorean identity collapses the square root.
  • Each substitution corresponds to a right triangle you can draw.
  • Always convert back to x at the end using that triangle.

Integrals of powers of sine, cosine, and tangent appear constantly in physics and engineering — Fourier analysis, signal processing, and wave problems are full of them. A few identity-based strategies handle them all.

Powers of trig functions do not integrate directly, but trig identities reshape them into forms that do. The strategy depends on whether the powers are odd or even.

Powers of Sine and Cosine

Odd-power strategy
If sine or cosine appears to an odd power, peel off one factor, convert the rest using sin²x + cos²x = 1, and substitute. The peeled factor becomes du.
Even-power strategy
If both powers are even, use the half-angle identities sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to lower the powers.
🧠 ANALOGY

The Pythagorean identity sin²x + cos²x = 1 is a currency exchange: it lets you trade sines for cosines whenever it is convenient. The odd-power trick spends one factor to set up a clean substitution with the rest.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — odd power of sine
Find ∫ sin³x dx.
1
Odd power: peel off one sine. sin³x = sin²x · sin x = (1 − cos²x) sin x.
2
Let u = cos x, so du = −sin x dx. The integral becomes ∫(1 − u²)(−du).
3
= −∫(1 − u²) du = −(u − u³/3) = −u + u³/3.
4
Substitute back u = cos x: −cos x + (cos³x)/3 + C.
∫ sin³x dx = −cos x + (cos³x)/3 + C.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — even power
Find ∫ sin²x dx.
1
Even power: use the half-angle identity sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2.
2
∫(1 − cos 2x)/2 dx = (1/2)∫(1 − cos 2x) dx.
3
= (1/2)[x − (1/2)sin 2x] = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4.
∫ sin²x dx = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.

Show worked solution

Show worked solution

∫ = x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C

Substitution undoes the chain rule; integration by parts undoes the product rule. It is the go-to technique whenever an integrand is a product of two different kinds of functions — like x·eˣ or x·cos x — that no substitution can crack.

When you face an integral that is a product of two unrelated functions, integration by parts trades it for a (hopefully simpler) integral. The whole method is one formula and one good choice.

The Formula

Integration by parts
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. You split the integrand into a part to differentiate (u) and a part to integrate (dv); the formula swaps the original integral for one involving du and v.
🧠 ANALOGY

Integration by parts is a trade: you hand over the hard integral and receive a different one in return. The art is choosing u so that du is simpler than u — then the integral you get back is easier than the one you gave up.

Choosing u: the LIATE Order

Pick u as whichever type appears earliest in this list (it differentiates toward something simpler); the rest becomes dv:

LetterType
LLogarithmic (ln x)
IInverse trig (arctan x)
AAlgebraic (x, x²)
TTrigonometric (sin x, cos x)
EExponential (eˣ)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — algebraic times exponential
Find ∫ x eˣ dx.
1
LIATE: Algebraic (x) beats Exponential, so u = x and dv = eˣ dx.
2
Then du = dx and v = ∫eˣ dx = eˣ.
3
Apply uv − ∫v du: x·eˣ − ∫eˣ dx.
4
= x eˣ − eˣ + C.
∫ x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C. (Check by differentiating with the product rule. ✓)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — the logarithm trick
Find ∫ ln x dx.
1
There is only one function — but write it as ln x · 1. Let u = ln x, dv = 1 dx.
2
Then du = (1/x) dx and v = x.
3
Apply: x ln x − ∫ x·(1/x) dx = x ln x − ∫ 1 dx.
4
= x ln x − x + C.
∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C. (A classic — worth memorizing.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find ∫ x cos x dx. (Let u = x, dv = cos x dx.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

u = x → du = dx; dv = cos x dx → v = sin x. uv − ∫v du = x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x − (−cos x) + C = x sin x + cos x + C.

∫ = x sin x + cos x + C
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find ∫ x e2x dx. (Let u = x, dv = e2x dx, so v = (1/2)e2x.) Work below.
Show worked solution

u = x → du = dx; dv = e2xdx → v = (1/2)e2x. uv − ∫v du = (1/2)x e2x − ∫(1/2)e2x dx = (1/2)x e2x − (1/4)e2x + C.

∫ = (1/2)x e2x − (1/4)e2x + C
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Choose u to get simpler, not more complex. For ∫x eˣ dx, picking u = eˣ would give du = eˣ dx and v = x²/2 — leaving a harder integral. LIATE keeps you out of that trap.

Key Takeaways
  • Integration by parts: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du — the reverse of the product rule.
  • Use LIATE to pick u (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential).
  • For ∫ln x dx, write it as ln x · 1 and let u = ln x.
  • The goal is an easier remaining integral — choose u so that du simplifies.
📊 FIGURE — Integration by parts: trade one integral for a better one
Split the integrand into u (something that SIMPLIFIES when differentiated) and dv (something you can integrate). The formula swaps your problem for uv minus a hopefully-easier integral. LIATE (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential) ranks good u choices.

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.

StepWhat you doWhere in this app

2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.

Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Techniques of Integration

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Integration by Parts

▸ Integration by parts ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du . You split the integrand into a part to differentiate (u) and a part to integrate (dv); the formula swaps the original integral for one involving du and v.

Trigonometric Integrals

▸ Odd-power strategy If sine or cosine appears to an odd power, peel off one factor, convert the rest using sin²x + cos²x = 1, and substitute. The peeled factor becomes du.

▸ Even-power strategy If both powers are even , use the half-angle identities sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to lower the powers.

Trigonometric Substitution

The Three Forms — Each form matches a right triangle. √(a² − x²) is a leg when x and a are the other leg and hypotenuse — so setting x = a sin θ just names the angle. You are reading the…

Partial Fractions

▸ Partial fraction decomposition Write a proper rational function as a sum of fractions with simpler denominators. For distinct linear factors , each factor (x − r) gets its own term A/(x − r) with a constant to be found.

Improper Integrals

▸ Improper integral (infinite limit) ∫ a ∞ f(x) dx = lim t→∞ ∫ a t f(x) dx . If the limit is a finite number, the integral converges ; if it is infinite or does not exist, it diverges .

"}, "CALC2/cheat/c2": {"body": "

📋 Applications of Integration

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Volumes by Disks & Washers

▸ Disk method Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis, each slice is a disk of radius R(x) = f(x) and area πR². The volume is V = ∫ a b π[f(x)]² dx .

▸ Washer method If the solid has a hole, each slice is a washer (a ring): V = ∫ a b π([R outer ]² − [R inner ]²) dx . Subtract the inner disk's area from the outer disk's area.

Volumes by Cylindrical Shells

▸ Shell method Revolving around the y-axis, each shell at position x has radius x and height f(x). Its volume is 2π·(radius)·(height)·(thickness). Total: V = ∫ a b 2π x · f(x) dx .

Arc Length & Surface Area

▸ Arc length The length of y = f(x) from a to b is L = ∫ a b √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx . Each tiny piece of curve is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs dx and dy = f′(x)dx.

▸ Surface area Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis generates a surface of area S = ∫ a b 2π f(x) √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx — the arc-length element times the circumference 2πf(x) it sweeps.

Work & Physical Applications

▸ Work integral If a force F(x) acts along the x-direction from a to b, the work done is W = ∫ a b F(x) dx . Each tiny displacement dx requires work F(x)·dx; the integral sums them.

▸ Hooke's Law A spring resists with force F(x) = kx , proportional to the stretch x (k is the spring constant). The work to stretch from 0 to d is W = ∫ 0 d kx dx = (1/2)kd².

"}, "CALC2/cheat/c3": {"body": "

📋 Sequences & Series

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Sequences

▸ Sequence limit A sequence {aₙ} converges to L if aₙ approaches L as n → ∞, written lim n→∞ aₙ = L. If no finite limit exists, the sequence diverges .

Series & Geometric Series

▸ Convergence of a series The partial sum Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. The series converges to S if the partial sums Sₙ → S as n → ∞. Otherwise it diverges .

▸ Geometric series A series where each term is a constant ratio r times the previous: a + ar + ar² + ar³ + …. It converges if |r| < 1 , to the sum S = a/(1 − r) . If |r| ≥ 1, it diverges.

▸ Divergence test (nth-term test) If lim n→∞ aₙ ≠ 0, the series Σaₙ diverges . (Caution: if the limit is 0, the test is inconclusive — the series might still diverge.)

Integral & p-Series Tests

▸ Integral test If f is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ 1, then Σ n=1 ∞ f(n) and ∫ 1 ∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge . Evaluate the (easier) integral to decide the series.

▸ p-series A series of the form Σ 1/n p . It converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1 — derived directly from the integral test and the p-test for integrals.

Comparison Tests

▸ Direct comparison test For positive-term series: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges , then Σaₙ converges (smaller than convergent). If aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 and Σbₙ diverges , then Σaₙ diverges (bigger than divergent).

▸ Limit comparison test If aₙ, bₙ > 0 and lim n→∞ (aₙ/bₙ) = L where 0 < L < ∞ , then Σaₙ and Σbₙ both converge or both diverge . Useful when the inequality for direct comparison is awkward.

Alternating Series & Absolute Convergence

▸ Alternating series test An alternating series Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ (with bₙ > 0) converges if two conditions hold: (1) the terms decrease, bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ, and (2) bₙ → 0. Both are required.

▸ Absolute vs conditional A series converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges. If Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it converges conditionally . Absolute convergence is the stronger, more robust property.

Ratio & Root Tests

▸ Ratio test Compute L = lim n→∞ |aₙ₊₁ / aₙ|. Then: L < 1 → converges (absolutely); L > 1 → diverges; L = 1 → inconclusive (try another test).

▸ Root test Compute L = lim n→∞ n √|aₙ|. Same conclusion as the ratio test: L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive. Best when aₙ is an nth power.

"}, "CALC2/cheat/c4": {"body": "

📋 Power Series

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Power Series & Radius of Convergence

▸ Power series A series of the form Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ centered at a. It converges for x within a distance R of the center — the radius of convergence — giving an interval of convergence from a − R to a + R.

Taylor & Maclaurin Series

▸ Taylor series Near x = a, f(x) = Σ n=0 ∞ [f (n) (a)/n!] (x − a)ⁿ = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + (f″(a)/2!)(x − a)² + …. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0.

Working with Taylor Series

Three Manipulations — Knowing the eˣ series is like owning a master template. Want eˣ²? Stamp x² into the template. Want the derivative? Adjust each piece. You reuse one known result many times over — one memorized series, substituted into, differentiated, or integrated term by term, replaces a dozen separate derivations.

📋 Parametric & Polar

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Parametric Equations & Calculus

▸ Parametric equations A curve given by x = f(t), y = g(t) for t in some interval. The parameter t determines both coordinates; eliminating t (when possible) recovers a relation between x and y.

▸ Parametric derivative The slope is dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt) — divide the two rates. This works even where the curve is not a function of x.

▸ Arc length (parametric) L = ∫ a b √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — the parametric version of arc length, summing tiny hypotenuses as t runs from a to b.

Polar Coordinates

▸ Conversion formulas From polar to rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ . From rectangular to polar: r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.

Area & Length in Polar

▸ Area in polar coordinates The area swept by r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β is A = (1/2) ∫ α β r² dθ . Each thin sector contributes (1/2)r²dθ — the area of a slice of angle dθ.
